p: Ezekiel dates this meeting to the seventh year of Jehoiachin's exile, the fifth month, the tenth day.
b: Ezekiel counts years from the first deportation in 597 BC (see 1:2). The seventh year is therefore 591 BC, and the fifth month (Ab) falls in July or August, so this is the first dated word since 8:1 (592 BC), about a year earlier. Scholars give the day as about 14 August 591 BC, but the conversion depends on whether the year is reckoned from spring or autumn, so treat the day as approximate (Block; Greenberg). Where Ezekiel's date-formulas stand in the book is a matter for the chapter page.

t: The elders who sit in front of the prophet
p: Leaders of the exile community come to his house, as they did in 8:1 and 14:1.
b: The elders were the heads of families and towns, the men who had run local affairs in Judah. In Babylon they kept that standing among the exiles (compare Jeremiah 29:1). Three times in Ezekiel they sit before him: here, at 8:1 and at 14:1. They want a word from the LORD, probably about whether the exile would end soon, since Jeremiah's letter had told them to settle down (Jeremiah 29:5–7). The LORD refuses their question (20:3, 31) and answers a different one: what their own history shows.

p: Ezekiel opens almost every oracle with the Hebrew words Adonai YHWH, "Lord GOD".
b: Koh amar Adonai YHWH is the messenger formula: a messenger began a king's message with "Thus says..." and then spoke in the king's voice (see the same formula in Samuel and Kings). Ezekiel adds the title Adonai "Lord" before the divine name, and does it about 217 times, far more than any other book. Because Jews read Adonai aloud in place of the name YHWH, the combination could not be spoken "Adonai Adonai"; the Masoretes point the divine name in this phrase with the vowels of Elohim, and tradition reads it "Adonai Elohim". Many translations print it "Lord GOD" or "Sovereign LORD". The Plain English Translation prints "the Lord GOD", with the name in capitals as elsewhere.
orig: כֹּה אָמַר אֲדֹנָי יְהוִה (koh amar Adonai YHWH)

t: The LORD swears by his own life
p: The oath formula "As I live" is the strongest oath God can take.
b: Chai ani "as I live" is a divine oath. People swore "as the LORD lives" (Judges 8:19; Ruth 3:13); God, having no one greater, swears by himself (Hebrews 6:13 draws on the same idea for Abraham). Ezekiel uses it often (for example 5:11; 18:3; 20:3, 31, 33; 33:11). The Hebrew continues "if I will be asked by you", the first half of an oath whose curse is left unsaid, so it means "I will certainly not." The Plain English Translation gives the sense and keeps "declares" (ne'um) for the oracle-formula at the end.

p: The Hebrew ne'um marks the words as the LORD's own utterance.
b: Ne'um is a noun, "an utterance", used for a word that comes from a speaker with authority. Prophets say it of the LORD ("the utterance of the Lord GOD"), and in Numbers 24:3 Balaam uses it of himself. In Ezekiel it comes at the end of or inside an oracle and tells the hearer that the whole saying, not just the prophet's report, is God's. The Plain English Translation renders it "the Lord GOD declares", set off by commas, as in Kings.

t: Three words for the ugly things
p: Ezekiel has three different words for what God hates: to'evot, shiqqutsim and gillulim.
b: To'evah (plural to'evot), "something abhorrent", is the word for what God cannot stand: idolatry, child sacrifice, sexual crimes, injustice. It is Ezekiel's favorite word for the sins of Israel and of Jerusalem (the plural appears over 40 times, beginning in 5:9; 6:9). It is a different word from shiqqutsim "detestable things" (20:7) and gillulim "filthy idols" (20:7). The Plain English Translation keeps the three apart. Here "the abhorrent things of their fathers" is a summary of the whole history that follows.

t: Idols in Egypt: a claim only Ezekiel makes
p: Exodus never says Israel worshiped idols in Egypt; Ezekiel says so.
b: In Exodus the Israelites cry out under slavery and the LORD rescues them. They are not charged with idolatry there. Ezekiel 20:6–9 (and 23:3, 8, 19–21) say they already served the idols of Egypt, and that the LORD planned to pour out his rage on them there, then held back "for the sake of my name". This is a widely made scholarly observation: Ezekiel rewrites Israel's earliest history to say that rebellion is as old as the nation (Zimmerli, Greenberg). Joshua 24:14 also speaks of gods the fathers served in Egypt. Readers who treat Ezekiel as a historian ask whether he had a tradition we have lost; readers who treat him as a preacher say he is telling Israel its own story in a harsher light.

a: I raised my hand in an oath
p: "Raising the hand" means taking an oath; it appears seven times in this chapter.
b: Nasa' yad "lift the hand" is the gesture of an oath (Genesis 14:22; Deuteronomy 32:40). Ezekiel uses it seven times in this chapter alone (20:5 twice, 6, 15, 23, 28, 42), each time of God. Five of them are oaths of rescue and grace (20:5 twice, 6, 28, 42: to choose, to bring out, to give the land), and two are oaths of punishment (20:15, 23: to keep a generation out of the land and to scatter them). Many translations render these as "swore". The Plain English Translation keeps the picture of the raised hand, which gives the chapter its drumbeat.

t: The LORD scouted the land, the Beautiful Land
p: The verb is the one used for the spies in Numbers 13: God himself surveyed the land first.
b: Tur "scout, spy out" is the verb for the twelve spies of Numbers 13:2, 16–17. Here the LORD is the scout: he looked over the land before Israel did and chose it. The phrase "flowing with milk and honey" is the stock description from the Exodus tradition. "The Beautiful Land" renders tsevi hi, literally "beauty it is, above all the lands". Tsevi means "beauty" and also "gazelle", the graceful animal (Deuteronomy 12:15). The same word is used of the land at 20:15, and the Plain English Translation gives it one name in both places. It is the site's name for the land wherever tsevi stands for it: Jeremiah 3:19, where the same word describes the land's beautiful inheritance, and Daniel 8:9; 11:16, 41 ("the Beautiful Land").
r: Numbers 13:2; Exodus 3:8; Deuteronomy 11:12; Jeremiah 3:19; Daniel 8:9; Daniel 11:16; Daniel 11:41

p: A second word for idolatry's objects: what the eyes rest on and love.
b: Shiqqutsim are things that cause disgust, mostly idols and their cult objects (Deuteronomy 29:17; Jeremiah 7:30). The phrase here, literally "the detestable things of his eyes", pictures people looking at idols and being drawn to them. Ezekiel's three words for idol worship are not the same word in different dress, and the Plain English Translation keeps them apart: shiqqutsim "detestable things", gillulim "filthy idols" and to'evot "abhorrent things". See the notes at 20:4 and 20:7.

p: Ezekiel's mocking word for idols; it sounds like a word for dung.
b: Gillulim occurs about 39 times in Ezekiel and only a handful of times in the rest of the Bible. Many scholars connect it with gelel "dung pellets", and the word sounds like galal "roll". The ancient Greek translators did not carry the insult over: they wrote eidola "idols". The Plain English Translation says "filthy idols" so that English readers hear the contempt. It is a word of contempt for what the nations treat as gods. It is not the same as 'elilim, the "worthless idols" of Isaiah.

p: The LORD's name can be made common in the eyes of the nations; that is Ezekiel's great fear.
b: Chilel means to make what is holy ordinary, to strip it of its set-apart status. Leviticus, on this site, renders the same verb "treat as common" (Leviticus 18:21: "do not treat the name of your God as common"). Ezekiel makes the verb the center of his theology: the LORD acts "for the sake of my name" so that it will not be profaned (20:9, 14, 22, 44; 36:20–23). The nations watching Israel in exile would think the LORD was weak. So the LORD rescues Israel for his own reputation, not for their merit.

a: the ones by which a human being who does them will live
p: Ezekiel's line comes from Leviticus 18:5 and returns in Romans 10:5 and Galatians 3:12.
b: Leviticus 18:5 says: "Keep my rules and my rulings. If a human being does them, he will live by them." Ezekiel quotes it three times in this chapter (20:11, 13, 21) as a promise the LORD gave and Israel refused. Nehemiah 9:29 uses it the same way. In the New Testament Paul quotes it in Romans 10:5 and Galatians 3:12 to contrast living by law with living by faith. Readers have long disagreed about what Paul means: Lutheran teaching on law and gospel, Reformed teaching on a covenant of works, Catholic teaching on justification and recent Pauline scholarship each frame his use differently, and this note does not choose among them. The Ezekiel passage gives the older, plainer sense: the rules were meant to give life, which makes the "not good" rules of 20:25 more shocking.

p: Sabbath is the one law Ezekiel names again and again as the test of loyalty.
b: Exodus 31:13–17 calls the Sabbath "a sign between me and you", and Ezekiel is the prophet who takes that idea furthest. He charges Israel with profaning the Sabbaths in every generation (20:13, 16, 21, 24), reminds the exiles of them (20:20), and ties them to the LORD's own act of making his people holy (20:12). Because Sabbath keeping did not depend on the Temple or on the land, it became more important for exiles, a mark of identity that traveled to Babylon. Some scholars see here the roots of the later Jewish emphasis on the Sabbath (Block; Greenberg).

a: in an oath that I would not bring them
t: The oath that shut a generation out
p: This is the wilderness verdict of Numbers 14, told as an oath of the raised hand.
b: After the spies' report the LORD swore that the generation that rebelled would not enter the land (Numbers 14:21–35). Psalm 95:11 and Psalm 106:26 recall the same oath. Ezekiel gives it the same form as the promises of 20:5–6: the same raised hand, but now against them. The chapter's order is exodus, wilderness rebellion, a second chance for the children (20:18–20), a second rebellion (20:21), and then the oath to scatter (20:23). Hebrews 3–4 uses the wilderness oath in its own way for Christians.

t: The children are told not to copy the fathers
p: Ezekiel 20 splits Israel into generations, as chapter 18 does.
b: In 20:18–20 the LORD speaks to the second generation in the wilderness and tells them not to walk in their fathers' rules but in his. This fits the argument of chapter 18, where a son is not condemned for his father's sin and may choose a different road. It also answers the exiles who said, in effect, that they were paying for what their fathers did (18:2). Here the children get their chance, and they too rebel (20:21). The picture is one of every generation answerable for itself and also of a pattern repeating.

p: One of the hardest verses in the Bible: the LORD gave rules that did not give life. Readers disagree what he means.
b: The LORD gives Israel "rules that were not good" and makes them unclean through the sacrifice of the firstborn. (1) A judgment. Because Israel refused the good rules, God handed them over to bad ones, like "God gave them over" in Romans 1:24. Rashi (as translated on Sefaria) says God delivered them into the hands of their temptation. (2) Their own decrees. Rashi notes that Targum Jonathan renders the verse differently: the people follow their foolish inclination and make decrees that were not good, and the LORD's "giving" is his letting them. (3) A law read literally. Exodus 22:29 says "Give me the firstborn of your sons." Zimmerli, Greenberg and Levenson, in different ways, link the verse to that law; Levenson argues that Ezekiel treats the old demand as a real command, once given by God and now seen as a horror. (4) The nations' customs (20:18, 32). Readers who hold with Paul that the commandment is "holy and good" (Romans 7:12) take (1), (2) or (4) and not a charge against the Torah. No reading removes the shock, and the Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew unsoftened.
r: Exodus 13:2; Exodus 22:29; Leviticus 18:21; Jeremiah 7:31; Romans 1:24; Romans 7:12

a: rulings they would not live by
t: The good and the bad rules as a mirror
p: The verse turns the chapter's refrain on its head.
b: Three times the chapter says the LORD gave rules and rulings "by which a human being who does them will live" (20:11, 13, 21). The fourth time, the words are turned inside out: "rulings they would not live by". Commentators on the chapter, among them Greenberg and Block, set the two passages side by side and read 20:25 as a deliberate reversal of the earlier promise; the hearer has heard "live by them" three times and now meets the loss of the life the first rules offered. Whether the reversal blames the people (they refused the life-giving rules and so were given others) or blames the LORD (he made the rules that would not give life) is the question the readings in the note above divide on.

t: "Pass over": the idiom of child sacrifice
p: The Hebrew "made pass over" is the verb used of giving children to Molech; here it is applied to the firstborn.
b: He'evir "make pass over" is the verb in Leviticus 18:21: "Do not hand over any of your children to make them pass over to Molech." Ezekiel adds "in the fire" in 20:31 and in 16:21; here the verse leaves out both fire and Molech, and speaks only of the firstborn, "every opener of a womb" (peter rechem), the exact words of Exodus 13:2. That echo is what makes the verse so disturbing: it ties child sacrifice to the law of the firstborn. The Greek (in Swete's text) has God as the one "passing through" and says "so that I destroy them". The Hebrew "so that I may horrify them" uses ashimmem, from shamem, a verb for being appalled or desolate. "Devastate" and "make desolate" are the other common renderings; the Plain English Translation takes the personal sense, "horrified", because the next clause has them come to know the LORD, which a people left desolate could not do.

a: They brought their offerings there that angered me
p: The words for worship are the same in 20:28 and 20:41; what changes is who is welcomed.
b: The phrase "soothing smell" (re'ach nichoach) is the Torah's phrase for the offering that pleases the LORD (Leviticus 1:9). Here Israel puts out a "soothing smell" on every hill, but it is at idol shrines; the offering is a ka'as "provocation", something that angers. In 20:41 the same phrase is reversed: the LORD will welcome his people "like a soothing smell". The chapter's last section thus gives back the words that the land's old shrines misused.

t: Bamah: a play on "go" and "high place"
p: A pun on ba'im "you are going" and bamah "high place".
b: Mah habbamah asher attem ba'im sham, "What is the high place that you go to?" The sound of ba'im ("going") plays on bamah. A bamah is a local shrine, usually on a hill. Ezekiel says the name has stuck, "Bamah", to this day. English cannot carry the sound. The Plain English Translation says "which means High Place". The Greek (Codex Vaticanus, Swete's text) does not translate but writes Abana, as if it were a name. Ezekiel's pun is also a sarcastic etymology: the place is named for the going.

a: make your children pass through the fire
p: Ezekiel says the exiles still do this "to this very day".
b: The charge is that the exiles' parents, and perhaps the exiles themselves, give children to the fire. Kings and Jeremiah describe such sacrifice in Judah (2 Kings 16:3; 21:6; 23:10; Jeremiah 7:31; 19:5). Whether it was still done in Babylon is unknown, and Ezekiel may be speaking of the whole people's continuing pattern. Some scholars see in "to this very day" a collective address to the house of Israel, not to the particular elders in the room. The practice is called by the name of Molech in Leviticus 18:21 and 20:2–5; Ezekiel does not name him in this chapter.

p: The elders may have wished to blend in with Babylon.
b: The people say, "We will be like the nations... serving wood and stone." The temptation of the exiles was to give up the distinct life of Israel, since the temple was far away and Babylon's gods seemed to have won. Isaiah 44:9–20 and Jeremiah 10:1–10 mock such idols. The LORD answers that it will never happen (compare 20:33): he will rule over them whether they like it or not, and bring them out again. The text does not say whether the elders' visit had anything to do with this saying; Block reads it as stating what the exile pushed them toward.

a: I will surely rule over you
t: A new exodus with the old words
p: "A strong hand and an outstretched arm" is the Exodus phrase, now turned into the means of a second rescue.
b: Deuteronomy uses "a strong hand and an outstretched arm" for the first exodus (Deuteronomy 4:34; 5:15). Ezekiel uses it for a second one: the LORD will rule over them as king (malakh) in the exile and bring them out. But the phrase comes with "rage poured out", so the second exodus is also a judgment on those who refuse to leave. Scholars call this the book's "new exodus" theme and compare Isaiah 40–55 and Hosea 2:14–15. A kingship that comes by wrath is a hard picture, and 20:35–38 supplies its reason: a trial.

p: A phrase found only here; its place is probably the desert between Babylon and the land.
b: Midbar ha'ammim is found nowhere else. Interpreters take it as the Syro-Arabian desert, the route home from Babylon; or as a figure for the place of the exile itself; or as a new Sinai, a place of trial for a new generation (20:36 compares it with "the wilderness of the land of Egypt"). The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew words. Hosea 2:14 is a related image: the LORD leads Israel into the wilderness and speaks to her heart.

t: Counting the flock under the rod
p: The shepherd's inspection: a picture of choosing and counting.
b: A shepherd counted his sheep by letting them pass one by one under his rod (Leviticus 27:32; Jeremiah 33:13). The image here is of an inspection that separates the faithful from the rest (20:38). The Greek (Codex Vaticanus, Swete's text) says "I will bring you in by number" (see the note on the variant at 20:37).

a: Go, each of you, and serve your filthy idols
p: The LORD seems to say "go ahead and worship idols"; most readers hear sarcasm.
b: The Hebrew is hard. Lekhu avodu is an imperative, "Go, serve". The most common reading is bitter irony: if you will not listen to me, go on, serve your idols, but do not use my name while you do it (Zimmerli; Block). Others see a judgment of abandonment like the one in 20:25. Still others read the verse as elliptical, "If you will not listen to me, then go serve your idols; but my holy name you will not profane any more", a promise that after the trial Israel will stop mixing the two. The Plain English Translation keeps the words of the Hebrew and its roughness.

t: Zion in a chapter about wilderness
p: The only place in the chapter that the LORD names as his own is the high mountain of Israel.
b: "My holy mountain, the high mountain of Israel" is the Temple mount, Zion. Ezekiel does not say "Zion" or "Jerusalem" here, and his Jerusalem is under judgment in this part of the book (chapters 21–24). Yet worship will return, and in the full book it will end in the new Temple of chapters 40–48 (see 40:2, "a very high mountain"). The verse also fits Isaiah 2:2 and Isaiah 56:7 ("my holy mountain"). The only acceptable place for the offerings is there, a contrast with the hills and green trees of 20:28.

a: You will hate the sight of yourselves
t: Shame as part of coming home
p: Ezekiel pairs restoration with remembering and loathing the past.
b: In 20:43 the returned exiles "remember" and "hate the sight of themselves" (literally "loathe in your own faces"). The same pattern runs through the book: 6:9; 16:61–63; 36:31. It is not despair, since it comes as a result of grace, not before it. The LORD acts "for his name" (20:44), not because they deserve it, and the shame follows as the right response to a mercy they did not earn. Compare the confession of Daniel 9 and Ezra 9.

a: The word of the LORD came to me
p: The Hebrew Bible starts chapter 21 five verses earlier than English Bibles do.
b: In the Hebrew Bible, English 20:45–49 is 21:1–5, and English chapter 21 is Hebrew 21:6–37 (English 21:1–32 = Hebrew 21:6–37). Chapter 21 in Hebrew therefore has 37 verses and English chapter 20 has 49 where the Hebrew has 44. This site uses English numbers everywhere, as in the KJV and most English Bibles. Jewish translations and commentaries (Rashi, Radak, the Jewish Publication Society) use the Hebrew numbers. The Greek, as printed in Swete's edition, is numbered like the English.

p: The verb hatteph "drip" is used of prophesying; the same verse has three Hebrew words for "south".
b: Hatteph "let drip" is a rare verb for preaching or prophesying (Amos 7:16; Micah 2:6, 11; Job 29:22). Ezekiel uses it at 20:46 and 21:2. The Plain English Translation keeps the picture. English "preach" loses the image of words falling like drops, slowly, on a listener. The verse also has three Hebrew words for the south: teiman, darom and negev. The Greek (Codex Vaticanus, Swete's text) turns the first two into place names (see the variant at 20:46).

a: every green tree in you and every dry tree
p: The fire eats both the green and the dry tree; the next oracle explains the pair.
b: The riddle is what the two kinds of tree stand for. The next oracle gives an answer: the sword will cut off "the righteous and the wicked" (21:3–4). Some commentators take the green tree as the righteous and the dry as the wicked; others take them as all of Jerusalem's people, young and old, whatever their state. Luke 23:31 may echo the saying, in which Jesus speaks of a green tree and a dry one on the way to the cross (Luke 23:31). Jewish and Christian commentators have read each in several ways.

p: The same Hebrew word means a parable, a proverb and a taunt; Ezekiel is accused of speaking in them.
b: Mashal (plural meshalim) means a comparison that carries a message: a story, a saying, a taunt or a riddle. Proverbs, on this site, renders it "proverb". Ezekiel uses it for his own parables (17:2; 24:3), for a quoted saying (12:22; 18:2–3) and, here, for what the listeners complain about. "Isn't he always speaking in parables?" is a complaint that his words are too obscure to follow, and so too easy to ignore.

a: The word of the LORD came to me
p: From here to the end of the chapter the Hebrew verse numbers run five higher than the English.
b: English 21:1 is Hebrew 21:6, English 21:32 is Hebrew 21:37. The words that begin this chapter are the formula that opens a new unit in this part of the book (21:1, 8, 18; 22:1, 17, 23; 23:1). Ezekiel's repetition of this opening is part of the book's voice, and the Plain English Translation does not smooth it into variety. Rashi, Radak and Jewish translations cite this chapter with the Hebrew numbers.

p: The Hebrew has "sanctuaries", plural: the Temple with its courts and rooms.
b: Miqdashim is plural. Ezekiel uses the same plural at 7:24 and 28:18. Most take it as the Temple precinct with its courts, rooms and altars, a single sacred area spoken of in the plural, as with the Hebrew word for "heavens" or "waters". Others think it includes the other shrines of the land. The Greek (Codex Vaticanus, Swete's text) reads "their holy places". The target of the oracle runs from Jerusalem (21:2) to "the land of Israel" (21:2–3), and in 21:20 the sword's road leads to "fortified Jerusalem".

p: In this chapter the formula is sometimes just "The LORD says this".
b: At 21:3 the oracle opens with koh amar YHWH "The LORD says this" without the usual Adonai. Most of Ezekiel's formulas read "The Lord GOD says this" (see 20:3). The short form occurs here and in a few other places (for example 21:9 reads "The Lord says this", with Adonai alone). The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew in each place and does not even them out.

a: my sword will come out of its sheath
t: The righteous cut off with the wicked
p: The sword takes "the righteous and the wicked", which sits oddly beside chapter 18.
b: Chapter 18 argues that the righteous live and the wicked die. Here the LORD says he will cut off both. Readers have long felt the tension. Rashi (on Hebrew 21:8, as translated on Sefaria) reads "the righteous and the wicked" as "the moist and the dry", the green tree and the dry tree of 20:47, so that the pair means everything in the forest. The Talmud asks the same question about the righteous who die with the wicked, but at another text: Bavli Shabbat 55a–b is built on the mark on the foreheads in Ezekiel 9:4–6, with 18:20, and speaks of "full-fledged" righteous and wicked. It does not cite this verse. Others read the pair as a figure for "everyone" (a merism, like "from the south to the north" in the next clause). The Greek (Codex Vaticanus, Swete's text) reads "the unrighteous and the lawless", which removes the problem (see the variant at 21:3).

p: The groan comes from the body: hips giving way.
b: The Hebrew is literally "with the breaking of loins" (shivron motnayim). The loins or hips were the seat of strength, so a groan from a breaking hip is the sound of a man whose strength is gone. Isaiah 21:3 and Nahum 2:10 use the loins in the same way. This is a sign act: the prophet shows the news in his body "in front of their eyes" before he says it aloud (21:7). The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew.

p: The same idiom is used in 7:17; its sense may be loss of control.
b: The Hebrew says the knees "go water" (telakhna mayim). The phrase also appears at 7:17. Most take it as "turn weak as water"; the Greek (Codex Vaticanus, Swete's text) translator reads it more bluntly, "will be soiled with moisture", as of fear that loosens the body. The Plain English Translation keeps the image of running water, which carries both. The news itself, "the report that is coming" (shemu'ah), is the fall of the city, which would reach the exiles in 33:21.

p: A short war poem in the voice of the LORD; its themes echo the Song of Moses.
b: Ezekiel 21:9–17 is a poem in short, driving lines. The sword is sharpened, polished and handed to the killer. Scholars note a likeness to Deuteronomy 32:41–42, where the LORD says he will sharpen his flashing sword, and the same Hebrew word for "lightning" (barak) appears. Some scholars suspect an older war song reworked here. The Plain English Translation sets the poem in lines. It is the book's most compressed war poem, and its text is among the hardest in the book: see 21:10, 13, 15.

a: The scepter of my son despises every tree
t: A crux: the scepter and the tree
p: The Hebrew is obscure; the line may speak of Judah's king, or of the sword scorning every rod.
b: The Hebrew reads "Or shall we rejoice? The scepter of my son despises every tree", and the second half is echoed at 21:13. "Scepter" is shevet (also "rod" and "tribe"); "tree" is 'ets (also "stick" and "wood"). Readers take "my son" as Judah or Judah's king (Genesis 49:9–10 makes Judah the scepter-holder) and "every tree" as every rod of discipline: the sword makes light of all lesser punishment. Some take "my son" as the LORD's own son, Israel (Exodus 4:22). The Greek (Codex Vaticanus, Swete's text) differs again. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew words and marks the line as uncertain.

p: Striking the thigh is a sign of grief or shock.
b: Slapping the thigh shows deep grief or shock. Jeremiah 31:19 uses it for Ephraim's repentance. Ezekiel is told to do what the people will do when the news arrives. The three gestures of this chapter, groaning (21:6), slapping the thigh (21:12) and clapping the hands (21:14) are all done in front of the elders as part of the message. In 21:17 the LORD claps his own hands.

a: For a test has been made
p: The meaning of this verse is uncertain; the Greek reads something quite different.
b: The Hebrew says, roughly, "For a test has been made, and what if even the scepter that despises will not be?" A test (bochan) of what? The Hebrew does not say. Commentators differ: a test of Judah's rod of rule, or of the sword itself, with "will not be" announcing the end of that rule. The Greek, in Swete's text, reads: "For it has been justified; and if the tribe is rejected? It will not be." The variation shows that even in antiquity translators struggled. The Plain English Translation is a close rendering of the Hebrew, not an interpretation.

p: A gesture of wrath in Ezekiel, done by the prophet and by God.
b: Ezekiel claps his hands in anger and contempt at 6:11; here (21:14) he is told to do it again, and the LORD claps his own hands in 21:17 and 22:13. In Numbers 24:10 Balak claps in rage at Balaam. The gesture closes the poem: the LORD will clap and let his rage rest (21:17). The sword that is "doubled" and "comes a third time" has been read as three waves of attack on Judah (in 605, 597 and 588 BC) or simply as a figure for complete slaughter.

t: Two rare words in the sword song
p: Two words appear nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible, so their meaning is a guess.
b: In 21:15 the words ibchat ("slaughter", or perhaps "glitter") and me'uttah ("wrapped up") are found only here. Ancient versions guess: the Greek (Codex Vaticanus, Swete's text) reads "well made" for the sword. Scholars think the sword is wrapped, drawn out of its wrapping or sheath, or wrapped in lightning, ready for slaughter. The Plain English Translation follows the commonest guess and marks the verse as uncertain.

p: Ezekiel draws a fork in the road, with the king of Babylon standing at it.
b: As with the brick model of Jerusalem in 4:1–3, Ezekiel is told to act out the message. He draws or marks two roads that start from one place, Babylon. One leads to Rabbah, capital of the Ammonites (modern Amman), and the other to Jerusalem. At the start of one road he sets a marker. The point is a decision: which city will Nebuchadnezzar attack first? Both Ammon and Judah had been vassals of Babylon, and both had been tempted to rebel; Jeremiah 27:1–11 shows envoys from Ammon in Jerusalem planning a revolt.

a: He asks questions of the teraphim
p: Arrows, household idols and a liver: the omens were Babylonian practice.
b: Three kinds of divination are named. Shaking arrows (belomancy): marked arrows were shaken from a quiver to give an answer. Asking the teraphim: household images used to seek a word (Genesis 31:19; Judges 17:5; Zechariah 10:2). Looking at the liver (hepatoscopy): a priest read marks on the liver of a sacrificed sheep. Babylonian and other Mesopotamian priests did this on a large scale, and clay models of livers survive. The Greek (Codex Vaticanus, Swete's text) has a "rod" for the arrows and "carved images" for the teraphim. Here the omen points to Jerusalem, and the LORD is seen to be steering the pagan king.

p: Rams, ramps and siege walls are the equipment of a Babylonian siege.
b: Assyrian palace reliefs from Nineveh, including the siege of Lachish, show siege ramps, wheeled battering rams and soldiers breaking walls. The Babylonians used the same engineering. The list here, rams, ramps, a siege wall, matches 4:2 and 26:8–9. The sound of the army's shout is the "war cry" of the verse. Jeremiah 52:4 and 2 Kings 25:1 record a siege wall built all the way around Jerusalem.

t: Whose oaths? A false omen in Jerusalem's eyes
p: The Hebrew leaves the "oaths" unexplained.
b: The verse says the omen will look like a false divination to Jerusalem's people "for they have sworn oaths". Whose oaths? The oaths of loyalty Zedekiah swore to Nebuchadnezzar (17:13–19; 2 Chronicles 36:13), which Zedekiah then broke; or the people's confidence in their own oaths of alliance with Egypt; or the oath-bound covenant with the LORD that they thought would protect them. In each reading the point is the same: Jerusalem trusts its protections and cannot believe the omen. The "he" who then "brings guilt to mind" is the king of Babylon, or, more likely, the LORD acting through him. (The Leningrad Codex's Ketiv and Qere for "divination" in this verse differ only in the vowel pointing of qosem, and the sense is the same.)

p: Zedekiah, Judah's last king, is called "leader" by Ezekiel and not "king".
b: Nasi is rendered "leader" on this site. The KJV and many versions say "prince" (a word that in English suggests a king's son). Ezekiel usually calls Judah's rulers nasi (12:10, 12; 19:1; 21:25; 22:6), though he also says melek "king" of them (17:12) and of the future David (37:22, 24). Some think the title keeps back the full royal dignity from the last kings. The "profane and wicked leader" is usually taken as Zedekiah.

t: Turban and crown: priest and king
p: The two items mark the high priest and the king; both are to be taken away.
b: The mitsnefet "turban" is the high priest's headdress in the Torah (Exodus 28:4, 37; 29:6), and the 'atarah "crown" is the king's. Both lose their place. The call to "lift the low and bring down the high" echoes the Song of Hannah and Mary's song (1 Samuel 2:7; Luke 1:52), though Ezekiel's "low" and "high" are the people and the king. Commentators differ on whether both items belong to the king or one to the king and one to the priesthood; either way the fall of the city ends both.

a: until he comes whose right it is
t: "Until he comes whose right it is"
p: Genesis 49:10 and this verse share a promise of a ruler to come; Jewish and Christian readings differ.
b: The line closes a three-fold "ruin". (1) A historical ruler. Rashi (Hebrew 21:32, as translated on Sefaria) says the one "upon whom I placed the mission" is the one God charged to carry out his vengeance, and reads "this too will not remain" as the kingdom passing from Jeconiah to Zedekiah to Gedaliah and not lasting under Gedaliah until Ishmael son of Nethaniah, who killed him. Radak (as read on Sefaria) names Nebuchadnezzar, who took authority from the guilty Zedekiah. The Targum of Ezekiel has the judgment not standing until the retribution comes through Yishmael bar Netanyah, whom the LORD delivers into the hand of the one punished. None of the three takes the line of the Messiah. The Messiah and Greek readings are in the next note.

a: To him I will give it
p: Christian readers link the line to Genesis 49:10; the Greek is as open as the Hebrew.
b: (2) The Messiah. Christian commentators have linked the line with Genesis 49:10, "until Shiloh comes", and read it of Christ; older commentaries such as Adam Clarke's do so, and Ellicott notes that Ezekiel here echoes Genesis 49:10. Other commentators accept an echo of Genesis 49:10 and a promise of the rightful Davidic ruler, as in Ezekiel 34:23–24 and 37:24. (3) The Greek. Codex Vaticanus (Swete's text) has "injustice, injustice, injustice I will make it, woe to her; such it will be until he comes for whom it is fitting, and I will hand it over to him" (see the variant). "For whom it is fitting" is as open as the Hebrew and fits readings (1) and (2) equally. The Hebrew mishpat means "right" and "judgment", and the line holds both.

a: A ruin, a ruin, a ruin
t: Ruin and guilt: avvah and avon
p: The Hebrew "ruin" (avvah) sounds like "guilt" (avon), the word of the whole oracle.
b: The three-fold "ruin" is avvah, from the same root as avon, "guilt, punishment", which runs through this oracle (21:23, 24, 25, 29, where the Plain English Translation says "guilt"). Published translators' commentary on the verse notes that avvah plays on avon in verses 23–25. The ruin is made out of the guilt. The three-fold repetition also gives the sound of the cries of distress. The Plain English Translation keeps "ruin" three times and shows the link in this note.

p: Ammon mocked Judah's fall; this oracle and 25:1–7 answer it.
b: Ammon, east of the Jordan, had been Judah's neighbor and sometime ally. The oracle speaks of "the scorn they pour out" (cherpah); Zephaniah 2:8 uses the same word of Moab's taunt and names Ammon's revilings beside it. Ezekiel 25:3, 6 charges Ammon with the same attitude in other words: "Aha!" over the Temple's profaning, and clapping and rejoicing. Ammon's king Baalis was behind the murder of Gedaliah in Jeremiah 40:14. Ammon was not spared: Josephus says Nebuchadnezzar conquered Ammon and Moab some years after Jerusalem fell (Antiquities 10.9.7), though the date is uncertain. Zephaniah 2:8 and Jeremiah 49:1–6 have parallel oracles.

a: Put it away in its sheath
p: The command may be to the sword, or the sword's fate is turned toward Ammon.
b: The Hebrew gives a command, "Put it back in its sheath!", and then switches to "I will judge you" in the place of Ammon's origin. Most take the first command as addressed to the sword (as in Jeremiah 47:6–7, where the sword is told to rest in its scabbard), the second to Ammon. The Greek (Codex Vaticanus, Swete's text) reads "turn back; do not rest in this place where you were born", a different division. "In the land of your origin" suggests Ammon will be judged at home, not in a foreign land.

p: The same fate is promised again in the Ammon oracle of 25:10.
b: "You will not be remembered" is a curse of erasure. Ezekiel 25:10 says the same of the Ammonites. In the Bible's world, to be remembered was to continue after death in one's name and line. The fire that makes Ammon "fuel" and the blood "in the middle of the land" are signs of a complete end. The oracle forms a pair with the rest of the chapter: the sword that falls on Jerusalem will fall on its neighbor too.

p: Jerusalem gets the title "city of bloodshed"; it comes back in 24:6 and 24:9.
b: 'Ir hadamim, literally "the city of bloods", has the plural damim, the word for blood that has been shed, so "bloodshed" or "murders". Nahum 3:1 gives the same title to Nineveh, and Habakkuk 2:12 to a city built by violence. Here it lists a wide range: murder (22:6, 9), judicial killing for bribes (22:12), and idols (22:3–4, where blood and idols are put side by side). The Plain English Translation renders the phrase the same way in 22:2 and 24:6, 9. Ezekiel is told to "judge" the city, to hold a trial as a prosecutor does.

p: The city is mocked by every neighbor, near and far.
b: "Unclean of name" (temei hashem) can mean the city has a name for being unclean, or that its name is spoiled. "Great in confusion" (rabbat hamehumah) can mean full of confusion or of panic. The Greek (Codex Vaticanus, Swete's text) reads these words as "famous, and great in lawless acts". The point is a reputation: the city once known as holy is known now for blood and idols. Lamentations 2:15 describes passersby whistling at "the city called the perfection of beauty".

a: They have made light of father and mother
t: A list that follows the Holiness Code
p: The charges in 22:6–12 line up with Leviticus 18–20, but Ezekiel does not quote it.
b: Nearly every charge in 22:7–12 has a counterpart in Leviticus 17–26, the Holiness Code: contempt for parents (Leviticus 19:3; 20:9), oppression of the foreigner (19:33–34), despising holy things and Sabbaths (19:30), slander and bloodshed (19:16), incest and adultery (18:6–20; 20:10–21), bribes (19:15), interest (25:36–37). Scholars debate the relation. Milgrom holds that Ezekiel knew and used the Holiness Code; Kohn argues that the dependence runs the other way; still others that both use older law. The comparison is worth making, but the direction of influence is not settled.

p: A phrase for eating a sacrificial meal at the hilltop shrines.
b: To "eat on the mountains" means to share in a feast at a hill shrine, where the meat of sacrifices was eaten before an idol. Ezekiel uses the phrase in 18:6, 11, 15 as a mark of the wicked. Deuteronomy 12 insists that sacrifice and sacred meals are for the one place the LORD chooses, not the hills. The next word, zimmah "depravity", is a strong word for sexual crimes (compare Leviticus 18:17; 19:29; Ezekiel 16:43, 58).

a: uncovered the nakedness of a father
p: A Hebrew expression for incest, not for seeing a father undressed.
b: "To uncover the nakedness" is the Torah's phrase for sexual relations (Leviticus 18). "The nakedness of a father" means a father's wife, as Leviticus 18:8 and Deuteronomy 27:20 show. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew expression and does not translate it as "dishonored", since it is the idiom, not the sense. The next clause, about a woman in her monthly period, refers to Leviticus 18:19. The verb for "dishonored" ('innah) does not say whether the woman agreed: the context in each case decides.

p: Two words for the profit a lender takes from a fellow Israelite.
b: Neshekh "interest" (literally "a bite") and tarbit "increase" are named together in Leviticus 25:36–37, which forbids both when lending to a fellow Israelite. Exodus 22:25 and Deuteronomy 23:19–20 forbid interest to a fellow Israelite. Ezekiel lists it in 18:8, 13, 17 as a mark of the unrighteous and here as a crime of the city. The law forbade lending at a profit to the poor, since the borrower needed help to survive. Interest charged to a foreigner was allowed in Deuteronomy 23:20.

p: The Hebrew verb can be read two ways; the Greek chose the second.
b: The Hebrew venichalt bakh can come from chalal "be profaned" (the Plain English Translation's choice, which follows the earlier uses of "profane" for the LORD's name and Sabbaths) or from nachal "take possession", "I will take my inheritance in you". The Greek (Codex Vaticanus, Swete's text) reads the second way ("I will take possession in you in the sight of the nations"). With the first reading the city is stripped of holy status in the sight of the nations; with the second the LORD claims it, as one claims a conquered land. See the variant at 22:16.

t: Dross: Jerusalem as a failed furnace
p: The refining image is turned upside down: no silver comes out.
b: Isaiah 1:22, 25 and Jeremiah 6:27–30 use the same picture of Israel as silver mixed with waste. In Jeremiah the refiner works "in vain" because the wicked will not be removed. In Ezekiel the image is more severe. All the metals are the waste ("copper, tin, iron and lead" are what is left over), and the furnace is not to purify but to melt them all. The Hebrew text reads sug in the Ketiv (the written text) and sig in the Qere (the reading tradition): two spellings of the same word for dross. Later prophets use the furnace for good (Zechariah 13:9; Malachi 3:2–3).

p: The furnace is the besieged city, filled with people from the countryside.
b: In 588 BC the villages of Judah fell one after another (Jeremiah 34:7), and refugees crowded into Jerusalem. Ezekiel's furnace is the siege itself: the LORD gathers the people into the city as a smith gathers metal into the fire, so that famine and war would melt them (compare 5:10–12; 2 Kings 25:3). Chapter 22 has no date. It stands before the siege-day of 24:1 in the book's order, and may belong to the months before the siege or to its first days.

a: a land that has not been cleansed
p: The Hebrew says the land is not cleansed or not rained on, and the Greek has only "not rained on".
b: The Hebrew (lo muttaharah hi lo gushmah) has two negatives. The first, "not cleansed", ties to the uncleanness of the land by blood and idols; the second, gushmah, is a rare word usually linked with geshem "rain". The Greek (Codex Vaticanus, Swete's text) has "a land not rained on", with only one idea. The two ideas are close: rain washes the land, and a land without rain is a land that nothing can wash. Some read it as a drought and some as a figure of the "day of indignation" (za'am) when no rain-like cleansing comes.

t: Prophets, leaders, priests, officials: the whole city
p: Four groups are accused in 22:25–29; Zephaniah 3:3–4 has a very close list.
b: Ezekiel names the prophets (22:25, 28), the priests (22:26), the officials (22:27) and "the people of the land" (22:29). Zephaniah 3:3–4 lists officials as lions, judges as wolves, prophets as reckless, and priests who profane what is holy and do violence to the law, in much the same words. Scholars debate which text draws on the other (the evidence cannot settle it), or whether both reflect a common way of describing a ruined city. The Greek (Swete's Codex Vaticanus) has "leaders" in place of "prophets" in 22:25: see the variant.

t: Priests' torah: teaching about holy and common
p: The priests' job was to teach the difference between the holy and the common.
b: Here torah is "law" in the sense of the priests' teaching and rulings on what is holy and what is clean (Leviticus 10:10–11; compare Haggai 2:11–13; Malachi 2:7–8; Ezekiel 44:23). The priests' failure to teach this difference is the central charge: a land that cannot tell clean from unclean cannot be kept clean. Ezekiel was himself a priest (1:3). The charge also explains the importance he gives later to priests who teach the people the difference between the holy and the common (44:23). Here torah means oral instruction, not a written code only.

p: This takes up the whitewashed wall of chapter 13.
b: The picture is of a wall that is shaky, which prophets coat with whitewash to make it look sound. It is told at length in 13:10–16, where the prophets "daub" the wall, and here it sums up the prophets' lies. "They say, 'The Lord GOD says this,'" is the false use of the messenger formula that opens so many of Ezekiel's own oracles (20:3): the same words can be true or false depending on whether the LORD has spoken.

t: 'Am ha'arets: who are "the people of the land"?
p: The term means different groups in different places; here it points to the landowners.
b: 'Am ha'arets "the people of the land" is used of different groups: the free landowners who put Josiah on the throne (2 Kings 21:24; 23:30), the landed class who share in the nation's government (Jeremiah 34:19; 37:2), and the general population (Ezekiel 7:27; 12:19; 33:2). In Ezekiel 45:16, 22; 46:3, 9 it means the ordinary worshipers. Here the people of the land are oppressors, robbers and cheats of the poor and the foreigner, so they are probably the landed upper class of Judah rather than the poor. The Plain English Translation keeps "the people of the land" in every place.

p: The LORD looks for a go-between and finds none; the verse is often used in prayer today.
b: The LORD seeks someone to "build up a wall" and "take a stand in the gap" so that he need not destroy. Psalm 106:23 says that Moses "stood in the breach" and turned God's wrath away. Jeremiah 5:1 is a search of Jerusalem's streets for one honest person, and Genesis 18:23–32 is Abraham's bargaining. Ezekiel 13:5 faults the false prophets for not repairing the walls. Isaiah 59:16 has the LORD finding no one to intercede and acting himself. Readings: the verse shows the need for intercession (the common use in prayer); or it shows that judgment came because no one at all could be found, which makes 14:14, 20, where even Noah, Daniel and Job could not save others, the same message in a different form. The Greek (Codex Vaticanus, Swete's text) lacks the wall and breach (see the variant).
r: Psalm 106:23; Jeremiah 5:1; Genesis 18:23–32; Isaiah 59:16; Ezekiel 13:5; Ezekiel 14:14

a: two women, daughters of one mother
t: An allegory, and the debate about it
p: Chapter 23 is a harsh story of two sisters; readers now debate how to read its violence.
b: The two sisters stand for Samaria and Jerusalem (23:4), the two kingdoms that came from one people. The chapter belongs with 16, with Hosea 1–3 and Jeremiah 3:6–11, where Israel and Judah are a wife and sister-wives. The sex and violence are the point of the picture and are what readers find hardest. Critics (Galambush, Weems and others) argue that the text uses a woman's body and her punishment as the picture of sin, and that this can teach readers to accept male violence as God's. Defenders (Block, Greenberg, Joyce) reply that the husband's role is a metaphor for the LORD's covenant, that the language shocks on purpose, and that the accused is the whole people, men included. Some scholars (Galambush is one) add that zanah in a marriage setting means "be unfaithful" rather than paid prostitution; the Plain English Translation keeps "prostitute" for the verb throughout, as in chapter 16, and the noun zonah (23:44, "as one comes to a prostitute") is a different word. The Plain English Translation does not soften the Hebrew and does not add coarseness. The chapter-page paragraph gives the debate in more detail.

p: Again the nation's youth in Egypt is described as rebellion, as in 20:5–9.
b: As in chapter 20, Egypt is where Israel began to go wrong. Chapter 16 puts the foundling's youth in the open field; chapter 23 puts it in Egypt. Neither story is in Exodus. For the claim of idolatry in Egypt see the note at 20:5. Several readers also link the sisters' time in Egypt with later alliances: Hosea 7:11 and 12:1 condemn Israel's courting of Egypt, and Judah's trust in Egypt in Ezekiel's own day (17:15; 29:6–7) is in view. The "youth" of 23:3, 8, 19–21 is the whole early history of the nation.

p: The sisters' names both contain the Hebrew word for "tent".
b: Oholah means "her tent" and Oholibah "my tent is in her". A tent is a shrine: the Tent of Meeting was the LORD's dwelling before the Temple (Exodus 33:7–11). Some read the names as a contrast: Samaria's tent was her own, Jerusalem's was the LORD's (the Temple, where "my tent" is). Others see only a sound-play. The Greek (Codex Vaticanus, Swete's text) spells them Oolla and Ooliba. The meanings were probably clear to Ezekiel's hearers, since names such as Oholiab appear in Exodus 31:6.

p: Samaria's "lovers" were the Assyrians, her protectors and masters.
b: In the 8th century BC the northern kingdom sought Assyria's favor. Menahem paid tribute to Tiglath-pileser (2 Kings 15:19–20); Hoshea paid it to Shalmaneser until he stopped (2 Kings 17:3–4). Earlier, Jehu is shown paying tribute to Shalmaneser III on the Black Obelisk (about 841 BC), where the king bows before the Assyrian ruler. Ezekiel's "lovers" language fits the prophets' habit of treating political alliances as unfaithfulness (Hosea 8:9; Isaiah 30:1–5). Assyria's gods came with the treaties.

p: Oholah's end is the end of the northern kingdom in 722/721 BC.
b: The text is brief. The site's 2 Kings says: "In Hoshea's ninth year the king of Assyria took Samaria" (2 Kings 17:6). Her sons and daughters were taken, and she was killed, "a name among women", that is, an example others speak of. The Assyrian king's own record says he deported about 27,000 people from Samaria (Sargon II), but the figure is open to dispute and the Plain English Translation does not rest on it. The point for Judah is the lesson: Samaria's fate was a warning that Oholibah did not heed.

p: Judah is judged more harshly because she saw the lesson and did not learn it.
b: Jeremiah 3:6–11 makes the same comparison: faithless Israel is shown to be less guilty than treacherous Judah. Ezekiel 16:46–52 makes Samaria and Sodom look righteous beside Jerusalem. Judah's alliances kept shifting: Ahaz called on Assyria (2 Kings 16:7–9), Hezekiah on Egypt and Babylon (Isaiah 30–31; 39), and later kings on Egypt and Babylon in turn. The charge in 23:11–21 is that she reached out to every empire in turn.

a: images of Chaldeans drawn in red
p: Ezekiel pictures red wall paintings of Babylonian officers.
b: The ancient Near East decorated palaces with painted and carved figures. Assyrian palaces, such as Til-Barsip and Khorsabad, had wall paintings of officials and soldiers, and Babylon later used glazed brick reliefs. "Red" is shashar, a red pigment (also Jeremiah 22:14, of a palace painted red). The scene is that Oholibah sees the pictures and falls in love at a distance. 4QEzek-a (4Q73), as transcribed by Abegg, Bowley and Cook, preserves parts of 23:14, 15, 17 and 18 (not 23:16), and what is not bracketed as restored agrees with the Masoretic Text. The word "Chaldeans" has a Ketiv and a Qere spelling in the Leningrad Codex.

a: sent messengers to them in Chaldea
p: The text probably describes diplomatic approaches to Babylon.
b: Hezekiah's meeting with the envoys of Merodach-baladan of Babylon (Isaiah 39; 2 Kings 20:12–19) is the best-known earlier contact. Zedekiah's reign had further embassies: he sent men to Nebuchadnezzar (Jeremiah 29:3), and his early reign was marked by loyalty to Babylon until he turned to Egypt (Ezekiel 17:13–15). The charge here is not that Judah talked with Babylon but that she courted it. The Plain English Translation reads the verse as a general picture of Judah's diplomacy. (4Q73 does not preserve this verse. The Leningrad Codex's Ketiv and Qere for "she lusted" differ only in the ending of the verb, and the sense is the same.)

p: The verb for tearing oneself away is used of Oholibah and of the LORD.
b: Naqa' means to be wrenched or torn loose, as a joint comes out of its socket (Genesis 32:25 uses a related idea for Jacob's hip). It is used of Oholibah's revulsion (23:17), of the LORD's own turning from her (23:18, twice), and of the hated lovers she "pulled away from" (23:22, 28). A lover's disgust and God's disgust are the same verb: the relationship ends because each pulls apart from the other. Some translations use "alienated" or "turned in disgust". The text uses two forms of the verb, yaqa' (23:17, 18) and naqa' (23:18, 22, 28), and the Plain English Translation gives them one English verb because the sense is the same. 4Q73 preserves parts of 23:17 and 18 and agrees with the Masoretic Text in what is not restored. The Plain English Translation uses the same plain English each time.

a: whose flow was like the flow of horses
t: Plain English Translation speech about the lovers
p: The Hebrew is deliberately coarse; the Plain English Translation is blunt but not crude.
b: The Hebrew compares the lovers' bodies to those of donkeys and horses (basar "flesh" is a euphemism for the male organ, and zirmah "flow" for emission). This is the language of 16:26 too, where Egypt is "big of flesh". The aim is not to excite but to shame: the lovers are described as animals. The Plain English Translation gives the sense with the same words, "flesh" and "flow", without adding to them.

p: These names are peoples on the edges of Babylon; their exact identity is uncertain.
b: Pekod, Shoa and Koa are named together only here, but Pekod appears alone in Jeremiah 50:21; Shoa and Koa appear nowhere else. Scholars compare Pekod with the Puqudu, an Aramean tribe east of the Tigris known in Assyrian records; Shoa with the Sutu, Aramean nomads; and Koa with the Qutu (the Gutians, an old name). These identifications are plausible but not certain. They show that the Babylonian army was a mix of peoples. The Greek (Codex Vaticanus, Swete's text) gives other forms of the names.

a: slice off your nose and your ears
p: A grim penalty linked to adultery in the ancient world.
b: Cutting off the nose and ears is attested in the ancient Near East as a punishment, including for adultery, and mutilation of the face was used on captives and rebels as well. Both pictures apply: the woman is punished as an adulteress, and Jerusalem's people as the conquered. Nothing in the Torah prescribes it. The Plain English Translation says what the Hebrew says; the horror is the point.

p: The cup that Samaria drank is handed to Jerusalem.
b: The cup of the LORD's wrath is an image for God's judgment on a drinker who staggers and falls. It appears in Psalm 75:8; Isaiah 51:17–23; Jeremiah 25:15–29 (all nations drink it) and Habakkuk 2:16. Jesus' prayer in Gethsemane about "this cup" (Matthew 26:39) and Revelation's cup of wrath (Revelation 14:10; 16:19) draw on this stream of imagery. In Ezekiel the cup is first Samaria's, then Jerusalem's: judgment passes from sister to sister, and "deep and wide" (23:32) says there is no end to it.
r: Psalm 75:8; Isaiah 51:17–23; Jeremiah 25:15–29; Habakkuk 2:16; Matthew 26:39; Revelation 14:10

p: A hard line: after drinking the cup dry, she chews its pieces and tears her breasts.
b: The verb garam means to gnaw a bone (Numbers 24:8). Here she gnaws the pieces of a broken cup, a figure for despair and self-harm. Tearing her breasts is a sign of grief and shame (compare Isaiah 32:12). The Greek, in Swete's text, reads quite differently: "I will turn away her feasts and her new moons". The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew.

a: pass over to those idols to be eaten
p: The children are said to be made to pass over "for food", language of burnt sacrifice.
b: As at 20:26 and 20:31 the verb is he'evir "make pass over". Here the Hebrew adds le'akhlah "for food", a word for what is consumed by fire, and the Greek (Codex Vaticanus, Swete's text) has "by burnt offerings" (dia empyrōn). The children are "mine" (they "bore them to me"), so the sacrifice is also theft: the LORD's children given to other gods. See Jeremiah 7:31 for the same practice in the Valley of Ben-hinnom.

a: they came into my sanctuary to profane it
t: The same day: worship at two altars
p: The women sacrifice to idols in the morning and enter the Temple the same day.
b: The charge is a mixture: the people kill children for idols and then go to the LORD's house, as if nothing had happened. Jeremiah 7:9–11 describes the same pattern: steal, murder and commit adultery, then stand in the house called by the LORD's name and say "We are safe". Ezekiel 8 shows the idols inside the Temple. "This is what they did in the middle of my house" is a summary of the Temple's corruption in Ezekiel's day.

p: The written text says "drunkards" and the reading tradition says "Sabeans".
b: The consonants of the written text (the Ketiv) are soba'im "drunkards"; the reading tradition (the Qere) is seba'im "Sabeans", people from Sheba or Seba in south Arabia, a trading people (Job 1:15; Joel 3:8; Ezekiel 27:22). The Plain English Translation follows the Qere. The Greek (Codex Vaticanus, Swete's text) has "men coming from the wilderness" without either name. Either reading fits a scene of a noisy, carefree crowd and visitors from the desert, and the difference is small. See the variant at 23:42.

a: Now they will go on prostituting themselves with her
p: The Hebrew of 23:43 is tangled; the Greek turns it into a question.
b: The Hebrew literally reads, "And I said of the one worn out by adulteries: now they will act as prostitutes, her prostitution, and she." The Ketiv and Qere differ twice ('et "time" or 'attah "now"; yiznuh or yiznu), which shows the scribes also found it hard. The Greek (Codex Vaticanus, Swete's text) reads "Do they not commit adultery in these things? And she too has played the prostitute". The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew as closely as English allows and marks the verse as uncertain.

p: The judges of the two women are "righteous men"; interpreters differ on who this is.
b: Three readings. (1) The invading armies act as the LORD's judges and carry out the sentence of the law on adulteresses; "righteous" is said with irony or because they carry out the law. (2) Human judges carry out the Torah's penalty (Leviticus 20:10; Deuteronomy 22:22–24), and the verse simply describes the law. (3) The faithful remnant who obey God, set against the unfaithful city. The judgment "on adulteresses and women who shed blood" in 23:45 joins two sins (adultery, bloodshed) found together in Ezekiel 16:38. 4QEzek-a (4Q73) preserves part of this verse and the following ones (23:44–47). For "they will judge" the transcription marks a word that differs from the Masoretic Text, and the line is partly restored, so this is a candidate difference and not a clear one.

p: The penalty is the Torah's; John 8 shows the same law in Jesus' day.
b: Stoning was the Torah's penalty for adultery (Leviticus 20:10; Deuteronomy 22:22–24). In John 8:3–11 the scribes and Pharisees bring a woman caught in adultery to Jesus and quote the law of Moses. Ezekiel 16:40 describes the same punishment for Jerusalem. The invading "crowd" (qahal, an assembly) here acts as the community assembly that carried out a stoning. Whether the later passage in John 8 belongs to John's Gospel originally is a separate question.

t: "Then you will know that I am the Lord GOD"
p: In a few places the recognition formula ends with "the Lord GOD" in place of "the LORD".
b: Ezekiel's formula "Then you will know that I am the LORD" ends with "the Lord GOD" (Adonai YHWH) in 13:9; 23:49; 24:24; 28:24; 29:16. The Plain English Translation keeps the difference. The formula is a trademark of the book: whatever the LORD does, whether judgment on Jerusalem, on Ammon, or on Egypt, or rescue of Israel, he does it so that people "will know" who he is. This is one of the book's most repeated statements (more than sixty verses; see the note on 5:13), and in each use the object of knowing is the LORD himself.

a: On the tenth day of the tenth month
p: The date is the same day that 2 Kings 25:1 and Jeremiah 52:4 give for Nebuchadnezzar's arrival.
b: Ezekiel dates this word to the tenth day of the tenth month in the ninth year. The site's 2 Kings says that on the tenth day of the tenth month Nebuchadnezzar arrived and camped against the city (2 Kings 25:1), and Jeremiah 52:4 gives the same day. Jeremiah 39:1 gives the year and month only. Jehoiachin's exile in 597 BC began Zedekiah's reign, so the ninth year of the exile is Zedekiah's ninth. On the count used here (Judah's royal years numbered from the autumn; Ezekiel's own exile years run from spring, as in the dates at 1:2) the day is January 588 BC and the city fell in July 586, about 30 months later. Some scholars count the years from the spring; the siege then still begins in January 588, but the fall is put in July 587, about 18 months later (see Thiele, and Hayes and Hooker). The choice between 587 and 586 changes the year of the fall and the length of the siege, not the day of Ezekiel's word. The book presents Ezekiel as knowing the day at once, hundreds of miles away; critical readers ask whether the date was added after the event. Zechariah 8:19 names the fast of the tenth month, still kept in Judaism as the Tenth of Tevet.

p: Two odd phrases: samakh "leaned" for besieging, and 'etsem hayom "the bone of the day".
b: Samakh means to lean or lay one's weight on something (the hand on an animal's head in sacrifice, Leviticus 1:4). Here the king of Babylon "leans" on Jerusalem; many translations say "laid siege", which is the sense but loses the picture of pressing weight. 'Etsem hayom hazeh, literally "the bone of this very day", is a phrase for "this exact day" (Genesis 7:13; Exodus 12:41; Leviticus 23:28). The Plain English Translation says "this very day". The Greek (Codex Vaticanus, Swete's text) reads the verse differently, "from this day". The Leningrad Codex's Ketiv and Qere for "write" differ only in a vowel letter: the Qere reads ketov and the written text lacks the waw. 4QEzek-c (4Q75) preserves parts of 24:2–3; in 24:2 its "write" is a restored word, so it cannot settle the spelling, and elsewhere what it preserves agrees with the Masoretic Text.

p: Ezekiel's name for the people of the exile: a house that rebels.
b: Beit meri is the book's fixed name for Israel, used from 2:5 on. The Plain English Translation keeps "rebellious house" every time. It names a stubborn trait (meri is from marah "rebel, be bitter") and sets it alongside "the house of Israel". Here it is the audience for a parable, as in 17:12. Their rebellion is the theme of chapter 20: this house, like its fathers, rebels at every stage.

a: Put the pot on, put it on
t: The pot turned against the proverb
p: In 11:3 the city's leaders said the city was a pot and they the meat; here the pot song answers them.
b: In 11:3 the leaders of Jerusalem say that the city is the pot and they are the meat, a boast of safety inside the city's walls, as meat is kept safe in a pot. Ezekiel's pot song returns the image: the pot is on the fire, and the meat is the people. Some see a direct reply to the saying in 11:3; others a separate parable that happens to use the same picture. Either way the meat is no longer safe, and the pot itself is the problem (24:6, 11–12).

p: Bones piled under the pot may be fuel; the Hebrew is obscure.
b: The Hebrew says dur ha'atsamim, "pile (dur) the bones" under it. The text does not say what the bones are for. They are usually taken as fuel for the fire, though the Hebrew itself does not say it. Because 24:9–10 speaks of piling up "wood" (ha'etsim), and "wood" and "bones" (ha'atsamim) look alike, one may guess that one word has replaced the other; no witness read for this part has "logs" here. The Greek (Codex Vaticanus, Swete's text) has "kindle the bones under them". The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew and leaves the use of the bones unstated.

p: A word found only in this chapter; the meaning is rust, corrosion or scum.
b: Chel'ah occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible (24:6, 11, 12). It is usually rendered "rust" or "corrosion", the green or black crust on a bronze pot, and by extension scum or filth. The Greek (Codex Vaticanus, Swete's text) calls it ios, "rust" or "poison". The pot is Jerusalem, and the rust is the blood and uncleanness that will not scour away. In 24:12 the pot wears itself out with toil, and the rust remains. The Plain English Translation keeps "rust" in all three verses.

a: with no lot cast over it
p: The pieces are taken out one by one, with no choosing: everyone goes.
b: The Hebrew says "no lot has fallen on it". Readings: (1) no one is chosen by lot, so no one is spared or picked; every piece comes out; (2) the pieces are taken out one at a time without a lot because the whole pot is to be emptied in the same way, as in the exile of the whole population. Casting lots was used to pick people, as in the scapegoat ritual (Leviticus 16:8) or to share captives (Joel 3:3; Nahum 3:10). The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew words.

p: Blood poured on the rock cries out, as Abel's blood did.
b: Leviticus 17:13 requires that the blood of a hunted animal be poured out and covered with dust. Blood left uncovered cried out for vengeance (Genesis 4:10; Job 16:18; Isaiah 26:21). The city has put its blood on a bare rock, where it can be seen. And God leaves it there too (24:8): the blood stays visible "so that it will not be covered" until vengeance comes. The pot, the rust and the rock are three pictures of one fact, a city whose guilt stays on the surface.

a: I will not change my mind
p: In this verse God says he will not relent; elsewhere the Bible shows him relenting.
b: The Hebrew lo enachem "I will not relent" uses the verb nicham, "be sorry, relent, change one's mind". Jeremiah 18:7–10 and Jonah 3:10 show God relenting when people repent, and Ezekiel 18 and 33 show that repentance can save. Here the siege has begun and the time for turning is past: the same God, in a different hour. Numbers 23:19 states that God is not a man that he should change his mind in the sense of breaking a word. The Greek (Swete) reads "I will judge you" in the first person for the Hebrew's "they will judge you" (see the variant).

p: Ezekiel's wife dies suddenly, and he is told not to mourn.
b: The death of the prophet's wife is the book's most personal moment. The Hebrew calls her "the delight of your eyes" (machmad enekha) and says she is taken "with a blow" (maggefah, a sudden stroke or plague). Readers differ. (1) A real event that the LORD used as a sign (the view of most commentators). (2) A symbolic action described but not necessarily performed, as some think of other sign acts. (3) Psychological readings. Some modern interpreters have used the chapter in psychiatric diagnoses of the prophet, a modern tradition whose critics say it reads Ezekiel as a patient and not as a prophet. The text gives no name, no age and no further word about her. It reports only that she died in the evening and that he obeyed in the morning (24:18). The Plain English Translation keeps its silence.

t: Mourning customs the prophet must skip
p: Ezekiel is told to omit the usual signs of grief.
b: Ancient mourners went bareheaded, barefoot and with covered face or upper lip, wept aloud and ate a meal brought by friends. David mourned with covered head and bare feet (2 Samuel 15:30). Covering the upper lip is a sign of shame or mourning (Micah 3:7; Leviticus 13:45 for a person with skin disease). Ezekiel must do none of this: turban on, sandals on, face uncovered, no cry. As a priest he was also limited by Leviticus 21:1–5, which restricts mourning for the dead; later rabbinic law on Leviticus 21:2 counts a priest's wife, if she is fit to marry a priest, among the kin he may bury (Bavli Yevamot 22b; Sifra on Leviticus 21). Those passages do not mention Ezekiel 24:16–17. His silence was therefore not a priestly rule but a divine order.

p: Literally "the bread of men": the meal friends bring to the bereaved.
b: Lechem anashim is literally "bread of men", and the Plain English Translation says so. Most take it as the meal of mourning that neighbors brought to a house of grief (Jeremiah 16:7); Hosea 9:4 has a different phrase, lechem onim, "bread of mourners", and says such food defiles. The Greek (Codex Vaticanus, Swete's text) keeps the literal "bread of men". Block reads it as the food brought by others; others as ordinary food. The gloss gives the usual sense.

t: The Temple, the second "delight of your eyes"
p: The Temple will be taken as Ezekiel's wife was taken.
b: The prophet's loss is the exiles' loss in advance: the same phrase "the delight of your eyes" (24:16, 21) is used for his wife and for the Temple. They will not mourn her death or the Temple's, because the blow will be too great for rites. The Temple was burned in 586 BC (2 Kings 25:9), and Lamentations 2:6–7 grieves that the LORD himself destroyed his dwelling and rejected his sanctuary. "The sons and daughters you left behind" are the children left in Judah when the first exiles went to Babylon in 597.

a: And you will do as I have done
p: The exiles will be unable to mourn: stunned, or forbidden, or both.
b: The sign is that the exiles will behave as Ezekiel did. Why? One reading is shock: grief so deep that no rite is possible. Another is fear: mourning openly for Jerusalem in a Babylonian town would be dangerous. A third is that they will be rotting in their guilt (24:23) and unable to turn the grief into repentance. Compare Jeremiah 16:5–7, where Jeremiah too is told to withhold mourning rites from a doomed people.

t: The prophet's name and the word for sign
p: His name appears only twice in the book; the sign is a mofet.
b: "Ezekiel" (Yechezqe'l, "God strengthens") occurs in the book only here and at 1:3. The word here is mofet "sign, wonder, portent" (also 12:6, 11; 24:27), a sign that points beyond itself, from the vocabulary of the Exodus plagues. The Plain English Translation uses "sign" for both mofet and ot. The LORD does not say Ezekiel's wife's death is the punishment for her or for him: she is a sign of what will happen to Jerusalem.

t: The survivor who will bring the news
p: The messenger of 24:26 arrives in 33:21–22, about a year and a half after the city fell.
b: The "survivor" (palit) is the fugitive who brings word of Jerusalem's fall. He arrives in 33:21, in the twelfth year, tenth month, fifth day (some witnesses read the eleventh year; see that verse). If the city fell in July 586 BC, the news came about six months later, in the winter of 586/585 by the reckoning used here. Between 24:27 and 33:22 stand the oracles against the nations (chapters 25–32); the mouth that 24:27 says will open is opened in 33:22, the evening before the survivor comes.

p: What the muteness of 3:26–27, 24:27 and 33:22 meant has been debated since antiquity.
b: In 3:26 the LORD makes Ezekiel's tongue stick to his mouth so that he cannot reprove the house; in 24:27 and 33:22 the mouth opens. Readings: (1) Total silence from 3:26 to 33:22, with speech only at the LORD's command (which still lets him deliver oracles). (2) Silence as intercessor or reprover: he could not argue with the exiles or plead for them, but he could speak the LORD's words. (3) A literary device. Some hold that it marks the book's three parts: judgment on Jerusalem (1–24), a silence for the nations (25–32), restoration (33–48). Old medical readings (catalepsy and similar) are a modern tradition, and critics say they treat as a disease what the text calls a sign. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew without explanation.
